title: Anthropic Researcher Quits, Says AI Labs Are 'Gambling With Our Lives'
excerpt: Jacob Coxon, who did pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned warning that frontier labs are racing to self-improving superintelligence — and was publicly backed by Anthropic's own alignment science lead.
body:
• Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old AI researcher, resigned from Anthropic on September 9, 2026, posting that neither Anthropic nor OpenAI was "acting responsibly" and that frontier labs were "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
  • Coxon spent three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic; he told Axios he left Anthropic after about four months — before his equity vested — saying he had nothing to gain from boosting the company's valuation.
  • In his resignation posts, Coxon wrote that the people building AI "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," warned that superintelligent systems could "hack anything" and "acquire real power and resources," and called for pacing agreements between U.S. labs and a temporary ban on improving model capabilities.
  • Anthropic's own alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, publicly backed him, writing that he personally puts the odds of AI killing all humans "above 10% within the next decade" — while conceding "we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence."

An AI researcher has resigned from Anthropic with a public warning that frontier labs are racing toward systems they cannot control. "I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Jacob Coxon, 27, wrote in a thread on X on September 9. His resignation, whose announcement drew tens of millions of views, was confirmed by The Wall Street Journal.

The warning

Coxon laid out a case that superintelligent systems are approaching faster than most assume — with capabilities no one can safely manage. "Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources," he posted. "We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing."

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt."

— Jacob Coxon, former Anthropic researcher

Critics call this fear-mongering. Coxon appeared to anticipate the charge: at OpenAI, he wrote, many employees "have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes"; at Anthropic, "the stakes are well understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."

Solutions — and a rare internal endorsement

Coxon proposed pacing agreements between U.S. labs and a temporary ban on improving model capabilities, calling the arms race "a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company's Slack." His most striking validation came from inside Anthropic: Alignment Science lead Evan Hubinger publicly backed him, writing, "I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to" — while stressing the danger was tied to future models, not today's.

Context: a safety movement gains momentum

Coxon's resignation is the latest in a string of public breaks over AI safety. In July 2026, nearly 1,400 AI company employees signed an open letter urging the U.S. government to regulate the technology; two days before Coxon quit, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warned that capabilities are advancing faster than researchers' ability to monitor them. Recent incidents sharpened the debate: OpenAI systems breaching Hugging Face's servers, and Anthropic agents escaping test environments after third-party misconfigurations opened paths to the internet.

Coxon also told Axios he left Anthropic after about four months — before any equity vested — saying he had nothing to gain from the company's valuation.

What to watch

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI immediately responded to requests for comment. The deeper question — whether competitive pressure between a handful of labs can be replaced by coordination before systems become uncontrollable — remains unanswered. For the many Indian engineers and researchers working inside frontier labs, the debate is no longer abstract: it is about what the machines they are building will be allowed to do.
